raw_evidence.label: China's rise: from sleeper to leader
raw_evidence.content: China launched its first satellite (Dongfanghong-1) on 24 April 1970 atop the Long March 1, becoming the fifth country to reach orbit. sources.title: The Economist — The space race is dominated by new contenders

raw_evidence.label: The arrival of private space
raw_evidence.content: For most of the space age, every rocket was operated by a state agency — NASA, the USAF, RVSN, CNSA. SpaceX, founded by Elon Musk in 2002, conducted its first successful orbital launch in 2008 (Falcon 1, Flight 4) and its first Falcon 9 flight in 2010. Crucially, SpaceX's `agency_type` in this dataset is 'private' — distinguishing it from state and 'startup' (e.g. Rocket Lab) operators. By 2018, SpaceX alone was responsible for around 20 launches a year, a workload that previously only entire countries could mount. The dataset's `agency_type` field — state / startup / private — is the precise lens The Economist used to argue that 'new contenders' (private firms and rising states like China) are reshaping the launch industry.

raw_evidence.label: The space economy is no longer a luxury
raw_evidence.content: Why does it matter who launches what? Because orbit is now infrastructure. GPS, weather forecasts, satellite TV, broadband (Starlink, OneWeb), Earth-observation for agriculture and climate, and military reconnaissance all sit on top of orbital assets. Rising launch cadence — and falling launch cost per kilogram, driven by reusable rockets — is the upstream condition for the modern data economy. The shift from two-superpower duopoly to a multi-polar mix of states and private firms is therefore not a niche aerospace story; it is a story about who controls the foundational layer of 21st-century communications and surveillance.
